[1] The summer I was sixteen, my father drove me four hours east and left me at my uncle Teodor's farm with a duffel bag and a promise, made to my mother more than to me, that the work would straighten me out. My uncle grew potatoes on two hundred acres of flat, pale ground that would have been sagebrush without the canal, and the work, it turned out, was pipe. Every field was watered by hand lines: forty-foot lengths of aluminum tubing coupled end to end across the rows. Twice a day the lines had to be uncoupled, carried one length at a time to the next set, and coupled again, so that the water could reach the next strip of plants.

[2] My cousin Marisa had been moving pipe since she was eleven. She was fourteen that summer and a head shorter than I was, and on the first morning she showed me how to drain a length by tipping it, how to carry it balanced at the middle so the ends did not dig into the furrows, and how to seat the coupling with a twist until the gasket caught. She explained all this once, without looking at me much, and then went off to her own line at the far end of the field. I decided she was unfriendly. It did not occur to me that she had been told to finish her line and half of mine before breakfast, and that she was doing exactly that.

[3] I was slow and I was proud, a combination that makes a person very tired. By the second week I could move a line in a little under an hour, which I considered respectable until I noticed that Marisa moved hers in thirty-five minutes and then sat on the ditch bank eating cereal out of a plastic cup. She never said anything about my time. She never said anything about much. When my uncle asked at supper how the north field was coming, she said "Fine," and when he asked me, I gave him a report.

[4] The trouble came in the third week, on a morning after I had been awake half the night reading. The set I was supposed to move to was the eighth from the road, and I counted wrong, or did not count at all, and laid my line down in the ninth. The sprinklers came on, the water hissed and settled, and I walked back to the house feeling that the day had begun well. The eighth strip went without water for two days in heat close to a hundred degrees.

[5] It was Marisa who found it. I learned this only later, because she did not come and tell me. She saw the leaves in the eighth strip going dull and soft at the edges, walked the rows until she understood what had happened, and moved my line back herself during her lunch hour, in the worst of the heat, and then moved it forward again in the evening so that the schedule would not show the gap. My uncle noticed anyway. He noticed everything about those fields, the way some people notice the weather in their own joints.

[6] He did not shout. He took me out to the eighth strip after supper and pulled up one plant by its stem, and we looked together at the potatoes clinging to its roots, small and a little misshapen, with a crease across them where the growth had stopped and started again. "That's two days," he said. "They keep the two days. You can't water it back out of them." Then he asked me who had moved the line, and when I said I did not know, he looked at me for a while and said that I did.

[7] I found Marisa on the ditch bank the next morning and tried to thank her, and the speech I had prepared came out as an accusation: why hadn't she just told me? She considered this with the cereal cup halfway to her mouth. Telling me, she said, would have taken longer than fixing it. Then she said, more carefully, that she had moved somebody's line back the summer before, too, and that the somebody had been her.

[8] I would like to say I became fast after that. I became a little faster. What changed was smaller and has lasted longer. I started counting the sets out loud, under my breath, every morning, a habit that embarrassed me then and that I still keep. And I stopped reading Marisa's silences as a verdict on me. They were not about me at all. She had simply learned, years before I arrived, that a field does not care what you say about it at supper.

passage_title: What a Coffee Mug Is Worth
passage:
[1] Give someone a coffee mug, and within a few minutes it will be worth more to them than it was before it was theirs. That, roughly, is the finding that made the "endowment effect" one of the best-known results in behavioral economics. In classroom experiments published in 1990, the economists Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, and Richard Thaler gave mugs to half the students in a room and nothing to the other half, then let the two groups trade. Owners were asked the lowest price at which they would sell; non-owners, the highest price they would pay. Standard economic theory predicted that about half the mugs would change hands, since the mugs had been handed out at random and there was no reason to think the students who happened to receive one liked mugs more than the others did. Far fewer traded. Owners typically asked for roughly twice what non-owners would offer.

[2] The explanation the authors favored drew on an idea Kahneman had developed with Amos Tversky: loss aversion, the tendency for a loss to weigh more heavily than a gain of the same size. If giving up a mug registers as a loss while acquiring one registers as a gain, then owners and would-be buyers are not really pricing the same thing. The seller is being asked what it would take to accept a loss; the buyer, what a gain is worth. Because the first looms larger, the two prices drift apart, and trade stalls even though nothing about the mug has changed.

[3] The finding traveled far beyond the classroom. It was offered as an explanation for why homeowners hold out for prices the market will not pay, why investors keep stocks they would never buy today, and why the starting point of a choice, such as the retirement plan an employer enrolls workers in unless they opt out, can matter so much. If ownership itself raises value, then whoever sets the starting point has quietly tilted the outcome.

[4] Not everyone was persuaded that the mugs revealed something so deep. In 2003 the economist John List took the question to sports-memorabilia shows, where dealers and collectors buy and sell all day. He gave participants one of two items of similar value and offered them the chance to swap. Inexperienced traders mostly kept what they had been given, as the mug studies predicted. Experienced traders swapped at close to the rate standard theory expects, as if the item in hand carried no special weight. Experience, it seemed, could wear the effect down. Or perhaps the people who never felt it were the ones who became dealers in the first place. List addressed that second possibility by returning to some of the same participants later, and he reported that their reluctance to trade fell as they gained experience.

[5] A different challenge came from inside the laboratory. In 2005 the economists Charles Plott and Kathryn Zeiler argued that the gap between owners and buyers might arise partly from how the experiments were run rather than from ownership itself. Subjects who misunderstood the rules, they suggested, might name an inflated selling price out of habit, the way one opens high at a yard sale, even though the procedure gave them no reason to bargain. When Plott and Zeiler explained the procedure carefully, let participants practice it, and kept their answers anonymous, they reported that the gap between selling and buying prices for mugs largely disappeared.

[6] Defenders of the original result did not concede. Some argued that the training in those experiments did more than clear up confusion: by teaching subjects to treat the mug as a number to be priced, it may have removed the very sense of ownership the experiment was meant to measure. Others pointed to later work in which a gap persisted under similar safeguards for some kinds of items, such as gambles with uncertain payoffs, even where it vanished for mugs. The debate has not ended so much as narrowed. Few researchers now claim that owning something has no effect on what a person will accept for it; fewer still claim that the effect is as large or as universal as the early mug studies suggested.

[7] What remains may be more useful than the original claim. A dealer who handles a hundred items a week and a student holding a mug she received five minutes ago are not, it turns out, the same kind of owner.

[1] For most of the last century, visitors to Port Ardrey were told that the paintings on its seawall had no authors. The wall runs for nearly half a mile along the harbor, and every few springs, when salt and winter storms have blistered the old paint away, the town's painting society scrapes a stretch of it bare and paints it again: boats, nets, the lighthouse, the names of the drowned. The guidebooks called it folk art, and the phrase did a great deal of work. It told visitors that the wall was made by the town in general and by no one in particular, which was charming, and which was not true.

[2] I spent four winters with the society's account books and with the photographs that harbor families keep in drawers, matching panels to the names of the people paid to paint them. The clearest hand belongs to Agnes Tolley, who painted on the wall from 1931 until the late 1950s. She is easy to find once you know how she painted water. Where others laid the sea down in smooth bands of blue, Tolley built it out of short, broken horizontal strokes over a red undercoat, so that the red flickers through the blue like light caught in the trough of a wave. Her water appears in more than forty of the photographs, and the account books record a payment to her for every one of those panels.

[3] Tolley appears in none of the society's own histories. Those histories, written by the men who chaired the society, list its officers, its fund drives, and its quarrels with the harbor board, and they describe the wall as the work of "the members." The anonymity that visitors found charming, in other words, had a particular shape. It was not that no one was remembered; it was that the people who wrote the record remembered themselves.

[4] Attribution will not damage the wall. Naming Tolley does not make the wall less communal than it is. It makes visible a person the community depended on and then forgot.

[1] My grandfather learned to paint the seawall from Agnes Tolley, and I learned from him, so I am glad her name is being said aloud again. I want to be careful, though, about what the name is being asked to carry.

[2] The broken strokes over red are not a signature. They are how the sea is painted on the Ardrey wall, and they have been since before I was born. Tolley may have invented them, and I think it likely, but she taught them to every apprentice she ever had, and those apprentices taught them to theirs. When my grandfather repainted a panel she had painted in 1938, he did not invent a new sea; he followed hers, stroke for stroke where the old paint still showed and by guesswork where it did not. I have repainted that panel twice since. Whose water is it now? A ledger can tell you who was paid in a given year. It cannot tell you whose hand you are looking at, because on this wall a hand is something you are given.

[3] Nor was the lack of signatures an accident of neglect. Painters were asked not to sign, and most of us still do not, because the wall is repainted on a schedule that no single painter outlives. What should be written down is the workshop: who taught whom, which panels were repainted when and by whom, how the sea came to be painted the way it is. That is a history with Agnes Tolley at its center, and it has the advantage of being true.

[1] When a whale dies in the open ocean, its body usually sinks, and on the deep seafloor, where food is otherwise scarce, a single carcass can feed a succession of animals for years, by some estimates for decades. Researchers who study these "whale falls" describe them in overlapping stages. First come mobile scavengers such as hagfish, sleeper sharks, and crabs, which strip away most of the soft tissue within months. Then a dense crowd of smaller animals colonizes the bones and the enriched sediment around them. Last, and longest, bacteria break down the fats stored inside the bones, and the chemicals they release support communities of their own.

[2] In 2002, a team from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, using a remotely operated vehicle to examine the skeleton of a gray whale nearly three kilometers down in Monterey Canyon, found the bones covered in what looked like a red shag carpet. The carpet turned out to be thousands of small worms, each a few centimeters long, rooted in the bone and waving feathery red plumes in the water. The worms belonged to a genus no one had described. The researchers named it Osedax, Latin for "bone-devourer."

[3] The name was a guess that turned out to be right, though the worms devour bone in an unusual way. An adult Osedax has no mouth and no gut. Its plume, colored red by hemoglobin, serves as a gill. Its lower body extends into the bone as a branching mass of tissue that researchers call roots, and inside the cells of those roots live bacteria. The current view is that the worm opens a way into the bone and the bacteria help extract nutrients from it, such as collagen and fats, nourishing their host in turn. How a soft-bodied worm gets through solid bone was unclear until researchers found that its root tissue is rich in proton pumps, molecules that move acid out of cells. The worm, in effect, etches its way in.

[4] The worms first collected were all female. The males, when they were eventually found, were not on the bone at all. They lived inside the females' gelatinous tubes, sometimes dozens to a single female, and they were microscopic: tiny creatures that seem never to develop much past the larval stage, living on the yolk they hatched with and apparently doing little but producing sperm. One hypothesis for how this arrangement arises is that a larva's sex depends on where it settles. A larva that lands on bare bone develops into a female; one that lands on a female becomes a male. Laboratory work has offered some support for the idea, though the question is not settled.

[5] The arrangement makes a kind of sense for an animal whose food arrives unpredictably. A whale fall is an island in a desert, and a larva drifting through the dark has no way of knowing when it will reach one. When it does, the first arrivals claim the bone and grow; later arrivals that land on those females are spared the cost of building a body large enough to feed itself, and a female that has settled is all but guaranteed a mate. Females appear to release eggs over a long period, a strategy suited to finding the next carcass by sheer numbers.

[6] Since that first discovery, Osedax has turned up far from California. Researchers have described more than two dozen species, from the North Atlantic off Sweden to the waters around Antarctica, at depths ranging from roughly a hundred meters to more than three kilometers. [1] When a whale dies in the open ocean, its body usually sinks, and on the deep seafloor, where food is otherwise scarce, a single carcass can feed a succession of animals for years, by some estimates for decades. Researchers who study these "whale falls" describe them in overlapping stages. First come mobile scavengers such as hagfish, sleeper sharks, and crabs, which strip away most of the soft tissue within months. Then a dense crowd of smaller animals colonizes the bones and the enriched sediment around them. Last, and longest, bacteria break down the fats stored inside the bones, and the chemicals they release support communities of their own.

[2] In 2002, a team from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, using a remotely operated vehicle to examine the skeleton of a gray whale nearly three kilometers down in Monterey Canyon, found the bones covered in what looked like a red shag carpet. The carpet turned out to be thousands of small worms, each a few centimeters long, rooted in the bone and waving feathery red plumes in the water. The worms belonged to a genus no one had described. The researchers named it Osedax, Latin for "bone-devourer."

[3] The name was a guess that turned out to be right, though the worms devour bone in an unusual way. An adult Osedax has no mouth and no gut. Its plume, colored red by hemoglobin, serves as a gill. Its lower body extends into the bone as a branching mass of tissue that researchers call roots, and inside the cells of those roots live bacteria. The current view is that the worm opens a way into the bone and the bacteria help extract nutrients from it, such as collagen and fats, nourishing their host in turn. How a soft-bodied worm gets through solid bone was unclear until researchers found that its root tissue is rich in proton pumps, molecules that move acid out of cells. The worm, in effect, etches its way in.

[4] The worms first collected were all female. The males, when they were eventually found, were not on the bone at all. They lived inside the females' gelatinous tubes, sometimes dozens to a single female, and they were microscopic: tiny creatures that seem never to develop much past the larval stage, living on the yolk they hatched with and apparently doing little but producing sperm. One hypothesis for how this arrangement arises is that a larva's sex depends on where it settles. A larva that lands on bare bone develops into a female; one that lands on a female becomes a male. Laboratory work has offered some support for the idea, though the question is not settled.

[5] The arrangement makes a kind of sense for an animal whose food arrives unpredictably. A whale fall is an island in a desert, and a larva drifting through the dark has no way of knowing when it will reach one. When it does, the first arrivals claim the bone and grow; later arrivals that land on those females are spared the cost of building a body large enough to feed itself, and a female that has settled is all but guaranteed a mate. Females appear to release eggs over a long period, a strategy suited to finding the next carcass by sheer numbers.

[6] Since that first discovery, Osedax has turned up far from California. Researchers have described more than two dozen species, from the North Atlantic off Sweden to the waters around Antarctica, at depths ranging from roughly a hundred meters to more than three kilometers. Experiments in which cow bones were sunk to the seafloor showed that the worms are not limited to whales; they will colonize the bones of other large animals when given the chance.

[7] The worms may also be old. Fossil whale bones roughly thirty million years old carry networks of small borings that closely resemble those Osedax leaves today, and some paleontologists have reported similar traces in the bones of marine reptiles from the age of the dinosaurs. If those traces were made by Osedax or a close relative, the genus did not depend on whales when it arose; it was eating bone before there were whales to eat.
